rv.q: This bizarre comedy grew on me; it keeps gathering in lunatic intensity until you surrender to its madcap charms.
The only hope of salvation for Moritz von Stuelpnagel's production is for the five actors to go at this muddle with terrific energy and manic conviction and this, to their credit, they do.
The show as a whole, though, lands somewhere between a smart, bold, insightful sketch and a fully developed play.
Hand on heart, it's hard to recommend.
But bright spots and a good cast don’t save the whole, a flimsy sketch of an idea promoted far, far beyond its means.
It strikes me as a coarse, crude satire that – not unlike The Book of Mormon – greets one form of excess with another.
Hand to God turns out to be just as smug, dull and unimaginative in its portrayal of these joke Americans, these hilarious hick Bible-bashers, as any patronising and sneering BBC documentary.
It’s all pitched at a very juvenile level.
Once the dizzying exposition is in place, Hand to God spirals towards blissful hysteria.
Either way, I'm with most of our younger critics and the majority of the audience who found it taboo bustlingly hilarious.
So let's come out, at least, on the show itself, the funniest and filthiest puppet glove punch-up I've ever seen.

There is no doubting this play is base, vulgar and utterly outrageous, but when the puppetry makes Avenue Q look like a nice show to take your grandma, then we're happy to switch gear for some laugh-out-loud silliness. The plot is thin, but progresses quickly enough not to care...The stand out, of c...
This unholy brew of grand guignol, sado-masochism and demonic glove puppetry thinks that it is being bold and iconoclastic when it is simply obvious and offensive.
Askins’ obsessive puerility won’t be to everyone’s taste – even if it does accompany a tale of growing pains – and his approach is frustratingly scattershot.
There really is nothing like it in the West End at the moment.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this profane puppet comedy, with some finding it hilariously outrageous while others dismiss it as coarse and aimless. The shocking puppet sex scene and Harry Melling's performance earn praise amid debates over its provocative satire.
